title: India Is 'Very, Very Close' to a Historic US Trade Deal — but a $500 Billion Target and New Tariffs Stand in the Way
excerpt: As the India-UK CETA prepares to launch on July 15, Washington says a bilateral trade agreement with New Delhi is nearly done — while a proposed 12.5% forced-labour tariff threatens to complicate the final stretch
body:
India's trade strategy is entering its most consequential month in years. On one front, a comprehensive trade agreement with the United Kingdom is set to come into force on July 15. On another, the United States says a historic bilateral deal is tantalizingly close — even as Washington slaps a proposed 12.5 per cent additional tariff on Indian imports that could upend the endgame.

## 'Very, Very Close'

US Deputy Assistant Secretary Bethany Poulos Morrison said last week that Washington is "very, very close" to concluding a bilateral trade agreement with India — a deal originally launched by President Trump and Prime Minister Modi in February 2026.

"This is going to open India's market of 1.4 billion to America's goods on terms that are reciprocal and mutually beneficial," Morrison said, pointing to the broader "Mission 500" target of $500 billion in bilateral trade by 2030.

The momentum is real. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in New Delhi in late June, with both sides describing the discussions as significantly productive. Bilateral trade in goods hit $149 billion in 2025 — a historic record and a $20 billion jump from the previous year. Indian companies committed $20 billion in new US investments at the SelectUSA Summit.

## The Tariff That Could Spoil the Party

But while negotiators draft closing language, the US Trade Representative's office has simultaneously proposed a 12.5 per cent additional duty on Indian imports under Section 301 of the Trade Act. The investigation, announced on June 2, accuses India and 59 other economies of failing to prohibit imports of goods produced with forced labour.

The levy would land hardest on India's labour-intensive export sectors — textiles, garments, carpets, leather goods and brassware — precisely the industries that have the most to gain from a trade agreement. The USTR is accepting public comments until July 6 and holding hearings on July 7, meaning the tariff decision could arrive just as trade negotiators try to close.

Trade analyst Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative noted an irony: the investigation is not about forced labour in Indian exports but about whether India blocks imports tied to forced labour elsewhere — a distinction that India's negotiators are likely to challenge.

## India Wants a Tariff Edge — and Will Wait for It

The biggest sticking point remains preferential tariff treatment. Goyal, speaking at the India Global Forum's UK-India Week in London, was blunt: India will finalise the deal only after securing a tariff rate lower than its competitors, particularly Pakistan and ASEAN nations.

"The whole deal was centred around that competitive advantage we got with that 18 per cent over our neighbours and competing countries," Goyal said. "That is why the deal was attractive for us."

Wendy Cutler of the Asia Society Policy Institute confirmed that the negotiations have reached a difficult stage. "Despite substantial progress made in recent meetings, concluding a trade deal with India is proving elusive," she said, pointing to a growing "trust deficit" between Delhi and Washington that has made wrapping things up harder.

India also wants assurances that the US will not impose additional tariff hikes after the agreement is signed — a guarantee that analysts say would be "a bridge too far" for the Trump administration.

## The UK Deal: A Model in Motion

While the US negotiations stall, India's trade agreement with the United Kingdom is preparing for launch. The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement will come into force on July 15, covering industrial goods, agricultural access, services and investment.

Goyal is in London finalising implementation details for both the CETA and the Double Contribution Convention, which will eliminate the double social security payments that Indian professionals working in the UK have long complained about — a direct win for the 1.5 million-strong Indian diaspora in Britain.

The UK deal offers a strategic template: it was concluded relatively quickly, delivers immediate commercial benefits and addresses specific diaspora pain points. For NRI investors and businesses, it signals that India is serious about integrating into global trade architecture beyond its traditional regional partnerships.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, these parallel trade tracks matter in several ways. A US deal would reduce tariffs on Indian exports — potentially lowering prices on goods from spices to textiles. It could also ease regulatory barriers for Indian IT services firms operating in America, a sector that employs hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin professionals.

The forced-labour tariff, if implemented, would raise costs for Indian exporters and could trigger retaliatory measures. Freight shipping rates have already jumped to two-year highs — the Platts Container Index rose 80 per cent in the past 30 days — as companies worldwide race to beat new duties.

The UK deal, meanwhile, offers a concrete near-term upside: reduced tariffs, eliminated double social security payments and easier market access for Indian professionals and businesses.

Both deals are pieces of India's broader strategy to diversify trade partnerships, reduce dependence on any single market and position itself as a reliable alternative in a fragmenting global economy. The next two weeks will determine whether that strategy delivers results or gets stuck in the gap between ambition and negotiation.

*Sources: The Indian Eye, Reuters, LiveMint, PYMNTS, Lexology*
